items.name: Kitesurf lessons at Ždrijac beach, Nin
items.description: Learn to kite in a closed lagoon where the water stays shallow far out from the sandy spit, one of the best-known learning spots on the Croatian coast. Courses go from a 2-hour 'Discover' session to independent riding (IKO certification), and the beach is a short ride from Sabunike.
items.howToBook: Book on kiteboarding-croatia.com (courses page / 'Book Now') or contact the school directly using the phone or email on its site. Prices booked in advance can differ from walk-in prices on the beach in high season.
items.priceDetails: 2026 price list on the school's site: Level 1 Discover 2 h €165; Level 2 6 h €485; Level 3 6 h €545; Level 2+3 12 h €845; individual hour €95; private hour €170. Course participants get 30% off individual lessons.

items.name: Windsurfing in the Nin lagoon (Kraljičina plaža / Zaton)
items.description: The steady summer maestral and the shallow lagoon make Kraljičina plaža, the long sandy beach that continues from the Sabunike shore, a classic windsurf learning spot. The Nin tourist board says windsurfing and kiting schools operate in the lagoon and rent high-end equipment.
items.howToBook: No current operator verified. Ask at the beach or at Zaton Holiday Resort, which the tourist board says runs windsurfing and diving schools.

items.name: 'Life on Mars' trail – self-guided hike on Pag's moonscape
items.description: This is most likely the user's 'life on Mars': a marked trail network (four trails, 16 km in total) through the bare white karst above Metajna on Pag. The bura wind has stripped the landscape so bare that the Novalja tourist board brands it 'Life on Mars'. Loops link Ručica, Beritnica, Slana and Seline beaches, and Croatia's first coastal via ferrata (about 100 m, rated difficult) crosses the cliff between Slana bay and Cape Sušac.
items.howToBook: Free and open all year. Download the trail map PDF from visitnovalja.hr/life-on-mars. Park at Ručica beach (Metajna). Bring plenty of water and sun protection, because there is almost no shade. The via ferrata needs a harness, helmet and via-ferrata set.

items.name: Guided 'Life on Mars' day hike or night hike under the stars
items.description: A local guide leads a 3-hour walk across the lunar karst from Ručica beach. The night version is a headlamp hike under a starry sky past Beritnica beach and the Stogaj rock column. There are also a guided via ferrata variant and a 3-hour evening kayak at Beritnica.
items.howToBook: Book online on Manawa (Sunturist listings) and meet at Ručica beach 15 min before departure. Transfer from Novalja costs extra.
items.priceDetails: Day hike from €25, night hike from €35 (headlamp included, ages 8+ with an adult).

items.name: Full-day Pag tour: Pag town, Life on Mars hike and Beritnica swim
items.description: A guided 9-hour loop from the mainland: Velebit views at Ražanac, photo stops at the Pag bridge, an hour in Pag town, an optional Gligora cheese tasting, a 2-hour Life on Mars hike from Metajna and a swim at Beritnica beach. A good 'whole island in a day' option for guests without a car.
items.howToBook: Listed on kroati.de and booked through GetYourGuide (tour ID t1306179). Free cancellation up to 24 h before.

items.name: Life on Mars Trail race, Metajna (Pag)
items.description: An annual spring trail race across Pag's moonscape, held since March 2017 and started to David Bowie's 'Life on Mars'. The 2026 (9th) edition on 29 March offered Light 7 km, Active 15 km and Challenger 25 km routes and drew more than 1,400 registrations from 17 countries. It is an easy reason to bring a running club or team in the off-season.
items.howToBook: Registration through the organiser. See the turistickeprice.hr announcements for the registration link. The date is usually the last weekend of March.

items.name: Nin healing mud (peloid) in the lagoon

location.name: Ninsko blato (Nin lagoon mud flat, beside Kraljičina plaža)

items.description: One of Croatia's best-known marine healing-mud (peloid) sites lies in the shallow Nin lagoon beside Kraljičina plaža, a short walk from the Sabunike shore. The local ritual is to coat yourself in mud, bake dry on the sand, then rinse off in the warm shallow sea. Roman bath finds suggest the mud was used in antiquity, and in 1960 the Zagreb Academy of Medical Sciences listed Nin as a climatic and thalassotherapy resort.
items.howToBook: Free to use on your own, traditionally in the morning in July and August. A supervised summer peloid programme led by staff of Opća bolnica Zadar (Zadar General Hospital) ran from early July to 31 August according to a 2023 Novi list article; the tourist board describes 10–20 day courses. Ask locally whether it runs in the current season.

items.name: Nin Saltworks guided tour and Salt House museum
items.description: Walk the working salt pans next to Nin's old town with a guide (45–60 min). Then visit the small Salt House museum with old tools, wagons and an interactive model of the reserve. On open days the tours, the museum and the shop are free.
items.howToBook: No registration needed. Turn up for a scheduled tour on an Open Door Day. 2026 open days: 5, 11, 18, 25 June; 2, 9, 16, 23 July; 6, 13, 20, 27 August; 3, 10 September. 2025 English tour times were 09:00, 11:00 and 17:00. Bring a hat and water.

items.name: Salt Festival, Nin Saltworks
items.description: The saltworks' free yearly festival offers treasure hunts in the salt fields, puppet shows, drawing with salt, and manual salt-harvesting and packing contests. It is one of the best family evenings of the summer on the Nin Riviera.
items.howToBook: Free, no booking. 2026 edition: 30 July (normally late July or the beginning of August).

items.name: Birdwatching at the Nin salt pans and lagoon (Natura 2000)
items.description: The salt pans and lagoon are a Natura 2000 wetland; Solana Nin records 158 bird species in the saltworks reserve (2019). Highlights are black-winged stilts, Kentish plovers, little egrets and kingfishers, plus migrating waders in spring and autumn. A small observation platform with parking sits on the west side, and late-afternoon light is best.
items.howToBook: Free, self-guided from the roads around the pans. The saltworks also lists wildlife information. Combine it with a bike ride from Sabunike.

items.name: SUP and kayak in the Nin lagoon
items.description: The lagoon is knee- to waist-deep and sheltered, so paddleboarding around Nin's island old town and its two stone bridges is about as safe and scenic as SUP gets. On maestral afternoons, paddle in the morning.
items.howToBook: No SUP or kayak rental or tour operator in Nin was verified. Guests may need their own boards, or the villa could keep a few for guests (see openQuestions).

items.name: Kornati National Park and Telašćica full-day boat trip from Zadar
items.description: A classic 9–10 hour excursion from Zadar's Liburnska obala, about 8:30 to evening, through the bare Kornati archipelago and Telašćica bay on Dugi Otok, with swim stops. Ticket-inclusive versions with lunch start at about €60. Cheaper trips leave out park tickets (Kornati about €16 adults, €8 children 4–12).
items.howToBook: Book online (Rezdy, Expedia, Musement and others). Check whether park tickets and lunch are included. Hotel pickup is usually not included, so drive or bus to Zadar.

items.name: Sakarun (Saharun) beach day trip on Dugi Otok
items.description: A full-day boat trip from Zadar's old town to Dugi Otok, then a bus transfer to Sakarun's long, shallow, white-pebble bay with Caribbean-coloured water. Some tours pass Tri Sestrice, Sestrunj and Molat on the way.
items.howToBook: Bookable on Musement, Expedia and similar platforms. Food and drinks are usually not included on cheaper tours.

items.name: Car-free island day: Silba or Molat by public catamaran
items.description: Skip the tour boats and take the cheap public catamaran from Zadar to Silba, one of Croatia's few car-free islands with no hotels, or to Molat, with deep quiet bays far from mass tourism. The Zadar tourist board recommends both for escaping the crowds.
items.howToBook: Check current Jadrolinija catamaran timetables: the Zadar – Silba – Mali Lošinj, Zadar – Premuda – Silba – Olib and Zadar – Molat – Ist lines. Day-return times vary by season.

items.name: Dolphin-watching speedboat trip toward Molat, from Zaton
items.description: A 2-hour speedboat trip from Zaton, about 3 km south of Sabunike, out between Vir and Molat, an area the listing calls a dolphin reserve, to look for wild dolphins. The boat idles quietly while everyone scans the water. Sightings are not guaranteed.
items.howToBook: Bookable on GetYourGuide (via kroati.de) and Travelocity. Typically part is paid online and the rest in cash on board.
items.priceDetails: kroati.de describes a €50 per person price paid as €20 online plus €30 cash on board, and lists the 'marine protected area and mooring fees (€30 per person)' under 'included', so the €30 cash part appears to be those fees. The same page's booking box shows 'from €25'. Treat €50 as the most likely total; €80 is not supported.

items.name: Scuba diving and try-dives in the Zadar archipelago

location.name: Diving Center Zlatna Luka, Obala kraljice Jelene, Bibinje

items.description: PADI and SSI centres around Zadar run Discover-Scuba try-dives, Open Water courses, and half- and full-day boat dives to Kornati and Telašćica. Bucket-list sites in the area include Premuda's 'Cathedral' caves and, for experienced divers, the wreck of the WWI battleship Szent István. Idula island off Ugljan is the closest beginner site.
items.howToBook: Contact the centres directly. Zlatna Luka is open daily 10:00–18:00 in summer and by arrangement off-season. Zadar Sub is open Mon–Sat 09:00–18:00 per its SSI listing.

items.name: Snorkeling at Duboka Draga
items.description: A rocky cove with clear water, rated for snorkeling, in contrast to the sandy, shallow lagoon beaches around Nin. Bring your own mask and fins, and expect a gravel road or footpath approach and a stony entry.
items.howToBook: Free public beach. Self-guided.

items.name: Sea fishing trips (Privlaka / Zadar)
items.description: Small-boat fishing charters run out of Privlaka and Zadar, from relaxed sunset trips to big-game tuna fishing out of Zadar. Pricing on aggregators runs from about $80 to $520 per trip.
items.howToBook: Search FishingBooker or Getmyboat for 'Privlaka' or 'Zadar'. Confirm the licence (a Croatian recreational sea-fishing licence is required) and the departure point with the skipper.

items.name: Team sailing regatta from Zadar
items.description: The Zadar Region Tourist Board promotes a one-day team regatta among the islands. Crews race friendly contests, each person gets a role (helm, trim, tactics) under a skipper, and the day ends at a beach club with sundowners, live music and food. No sailing experience is needed.
items.howToBook: Arrange through a Zadar incentive agency or charter company. The tourist board's incentive desk is +385 23 315 316 (as published on zadar.hr) and the page links to its 'Agencies and services' list.

items.name: Horse riding and pony rides near Nin (Zaton)
items.description: The Nin tourist board says a local equestrian club offers recreational rides for children and adults, riding courses and therapeutic riding. An older listing places a 'Nin Horse Centre' at Zaton with pony rides and a beach ride. The board also mentions a donkey farm nearby, reachable by bike, with donkey rides and donkey-milk tasting.
items.howToBook: Contact details are not verified. Ask the Nin tourist board or Zaton Holiday Resort reception.

items.name: 4-hour horseback ride around Vrana Lake Nature Park
items.description: A 4-hour guided ride around Croatia's largest natural lake, starting at the Vrana agricultural estate, listed by the Zadar Region Tourist Board with Ilirija Travel. Closer to Sabunike, the Mićanovi dvori rural estate near Obrovac offers 45-minute rides.
items.howToBook: Book through Ilirija Travel (ilirijabiograd.com). For Mićanovi dvori, go through Riva Rafting Centar, which lists horseback riding among its activities.

items.name: Rafting and kayaking the Zrmanja canyon
items.description: A roughly 14.5 km run through the limestone canyon of the Zrmanja, with waterfalls, swim stops and the famous 'Winnetou' scenery. Big rafts (6–12 people) run when the water is high, mostly October to mid-May. In summer, when the water is low, the trip switches to kayak safaris. Wetsuit, helmet, life jacket, guide and park fee are included.
items.howToBook: Book through FareHarbor via riva-rafting-centar.hr, or by phone or email as listed on the operator's site. Tours start from Kaštel Žegarski.
items.priceDetails: Manawa lists the trip 'from €50'. Expedia shows about $64 per adult (guide, gear, insurance and nature-park fee included; lunch and transfer excluded).

items.name: Hiking Paklenica National Park (Velebit)
items.description: Two dramatic limestone gorges, Velika and Mala Paklenica, cut into Velebit just across the Velebit channel from Pag. Trails run up Velika Paklenica past the 350 m wall of Anića kuk into the Velebit massif. A 1-day adult ticket costs €5–10 depending on the season.
items.howToBook: Buy tickets at the park entrance. Individuals need no prior announcement. The park is open 06:00–20:30 (per a guide listing).
items.priceDetails: Official 2026 price list, adult 1-day: €5 (Jan, Feb, Nov, Dec), €8 (Mar, Apr, Oct), €10 (May–Sep). Children 7–18: €2.50 / €4 / €5. Under-7s free. 3-day passes €10 / €16 / €20. Vehicle vignette €3–5.

items.name: Rock climbing in Paklenica (Anića kuk big wall and sport crags)
items.description: Croatia's premier climbing area: the basic park ticket covers about 600 equipped routes graded 3 to 8b+/8c, from single-pitch sport crags at the gorge entrance to multi-pitch lines up to 350 m on Anića kuk. The prime season runs from April to late October. Anića kuk stays shaded in the morning, and the sunny Crljenica sector works even in winter.
items.howToBook: Climbing is included in the park ticket. Climbing is prohibited in some zones, such as Mala Paklenica and Debeli kuk. The guidebook is by Boris Čujić (2024 edition).

items.name: Wine tasting at Kraljevski Vinogradi (Petrčane)
items.description: A hilltop estate above Punta Skala in Petrčane, about 7 km south of Sabunike in a straight line, with Adriatic views and more than 300,000 vines. The tasting room and konoba pour Pošip, Plavac Mali and Crljenak (Zinfandel's Croatian ancestor) with local snacks, and the konoba hosts team-building events and celebrations.
items.howToBook: Contact the winery through its official site (the phone and email are listed there). A guide says tastings run 11:00–16:00 daily without booking for groups under 10. For wine & dine, book through Orioly.

items.name: Zadar wine route – Ravni Kotari family wineries
items.description: Inland Ravni Kotari is the Zadar region's wine and olive country. Škaulj in Nadin pours Merlot, Syrah and Maraština in a Dalmatian stone tasting room. MasVin in Polača pairs organic wine with its own olive oils and fig products, year-round. On Pag, Vina otoka Paga serves the island's native Gegić with an oenologist (booking required).
items.howToBook: Contact each winery directly. Several Zadar agencies also sell 'hinterland wine route' tours combining Degarra, Kraljevski Vinogradi and Fiolić.

items.name: Lun ancient olive groves (Pag)
items.description: At the northern tip of Pag, around 80,000 wild olive trees grow between dry-stone walls. More than 1,000 are over 1,000 years old, and the oldest is believed to be about 1,600 years old. The groves have been a protected botanical reserve since 1963. Villagers still hand-pick the olives in late autumn, and the oil is known for its clean, gentle taste.
items.howToBook: Free to walk. Visitor-centre, entry-fee or tasting details are not verified; Terrapark describes the groves but lists no fee or tasting.

items.name: Olive harvest and tasting experience (Ljubač, near Nin)

operators.name: 'Be a Local' private olive-harvest tour (via byFood)

items.description: A private half-day in an olive grove at Ljubač, just east of Nin. You pick olives alongside an expert taster, learn to taste oil properly, and finish with a lunch built around local olive oils. In October and November the whole region, from Ravni Kotari to Ugljan and Pašman, is in harvest mode.
items.howToBook: Book on byFood or Expedia (private, from Zadar). For year-round oil tastings, try MasVin (Polača).

items.name: Home cooking class: peka and kroštule (Ninski Stanovi)

operators.name: Ninski Stanovi Cooking Class Experience (via byFood)

items.description: A hands-on class in a family home a few kilometres from Sabunike. You learn to cook meat or vegetables 'under the bell' (peka) and fry kroštule pastries, then taste homemade liqueurs. In English, for 1–8 guests.
items.howToBook: Book on byFood. Free cancellation up to 24 h before.

items.name: Zadar market tour and Dalmatian cooking class
items.description: Meet at a café on Zadar's Narodni trg, shop for ingredients at the city market, then cook Dalmatian dishes at your own station with a professional chef. Guests help design the menu.
items.howToBook: Book on Cookly. Bookings are confirmed within 24 h, with a full refund 48 h ahead.

items.name: Gligora cheese dairy tour and tasting (Kolan, Pag)
items.description: Tour the family dairy that has made Paški sir in Kolan since 1918. You see production, walk into maturing caves holding up to 200 tonnes of cheese, and finish with a tasting of award-winning Pag cheese. It pairs naturally with the Life on Mars hike on the same day.
items.howToBook: Guided tours in English, Croatian and German, Mon–Sat 09:30–16:00 (2026 schedule from 20 April). Groups over 8 must book ahead.

items.name: Zrće beach clubs, Novalja (Pag)
items.description: Croatia's open-air party strip, 2 km from Novalja. Papaya, Kalypso (the original), Noa and Aquarius run after-beach parties from the afternoon and big DJ nights through the summer, and spring-break festivals fill May and early June. Sabunike offers a quiet, cheaper base for groups who want Zrće nights without sleeping next to the clubs.
items.howToBook: Tickets go through each club or festival (spring-break events are sold via ticket platforms). A summer bus runs Novalja – Zrće.

items.name: Cycling the flat Nin Riviera (110 km of marked routes)
items.description: The Nin tourist board counts 110 km of marked cycling routes around Nin. The flat lagoon roads link Sabunike, Kraljičina plaža, the salt pans, Nin's island old town and the Ninski Stanovi or Zaton villages, so you can easily build a heritage-and-birds loop.
items.howToBook: Self-guided. See the separate cycling research file for routes and rentals.

items.name: Our Lady of Zečevo pilgrimage and procession, Nin
items.description: A 500-year-old tradition marking a 1516 apparition of the Virgin on the islet of Zečevo. On 5 May pilgrims go to the islet on foot and by boat, and Zečevo becomes part of the mainland at low tide. The main feast, with a procession through Nin's decorated streets, is on the first Monday before Ascension. A third celebration falls on 5 August.
items.howToBook: Free and public.

items.name: Festival of Sun and Light, Church of the Holy Cross, Nin
items.description: On the first day of summer, the pre-Romanesque Holy Cross church, nicknamed 'the smallest cathedral in the world', becomes a giant sundial. Light through its oval openings is aligned to the solstices and equinoxes. Talks and creative workshops accompany the light show.
items.howToBook: Check the Nin tourist board calendar near 21 June.

items.name: Ninska šokolijada – šokol curing competition, Nin
items.description: Held since 2003, this July contest crowns the best maker of šokol, Nin's signature dry-cured, smoked pork neck. The meat is handed out to competitors at the start of the year and judged in summer with tastings and festivities. Note that šokol is a cured meat, not chocolate.
items.howToBook: Free public event. Check the date with the Nin tourist board.

items.name: Nin Patron Saints' Days (St Marcela and St Anselm)

location.name: Church of St Anselm (former cathedral), Nin

items.description: On 25–26 August, Nin celebrates its patrons with church ceremonies around precious early-Christian reliquaries in the former cathedral, followed by the town's late-summer fiesta.
items.howToBook: Free and public.

items.name: Night of Privlaka Fishermen and Sabunjaras
items.description: This is Privlaka's own summer evening, in the villa's home municipality. Photo exhibitions and films celebrate the village's fishermen and its 'sabunjari', with local food and klapa singing.
items.howToBook: Free public event. 2026 date: 10 July.

items.name: Pag Summer Carnival (Pag town)

location.name: Pag town, Trg Petra Krešimira IV

items.description: A traditional carnival running for more than 60 years, held over four days in late July on Pag town's main square. It features a costume parade, the handing of the town keys to the carnival prince and the Pag kolo folk dance. Pag also holds a traditional winter carnival.
items.howToBook: Free public event. Check the Pag Tourist Board for dates (2023: 26–29 July; 2019: from 22 July).

items.name: Cheese Festival, Kolan (Pag)
items.description: Held on the last Friday of August, the festival brings together the producers of PDO-protected Pag cheese in its home village, Kolan, with tastings and a cultural and entertainment programme.
items.howToBook: Public event, held on the last Friday of August; for 2026 that falls on 28 August (calculated, not announced).

items.name: Full Moon Festival, Zadar Riva
items.description: For a few nights around the August full moon, Zadar's waterfront is lit only by torches, candles and the moon. Boats become floating markets selling fish, mussels, figs, cheese and rakija, with klapa singing and folklore on the Riva.
items.howToBook: Free public event. 2026 dates: 6–9 August (zadar.hr).

items.name: Musical Evenings in St Donatus, Zadar
items.description: A long-running summer series of classical and early-music concerts in and around the round pre-Romanesque church of St Donatus. The 2026 edition was the 66th, from 5 July to 6 August, with tickets from €5 to €25.
items.howToBook: Tickets through donat-festival.com.

windSeasons.spot: Nin lagoon – Ždrijac and Kraljičina plaža
windSeasons.summary: Mild thermal maestral (NW) from May to October is the beginner season: it typically builds late morning, peaks early afternoon and drops toward sunset. The shallow, closed lagoon makes Ždrijac a well-known learning spot. Spring and autumn bring stronger, more variable days (jugo from SE, bura from NE) that suit experienced riders. Winter is dominated by bura, which is strongest and most dangerous in the Nin bay area. No station-based monthly statistics were found for Nin: Windfinder shows none for Zadar Airport, and its annual figure (ESE, avg ~7 kn, gusts to 27 kn) is a land station and not representative of the lagoon.
windSeasons.schoolSeason: Kiteboarding Croatia (Ždrijac) states it is open every day from May until late October.

openQuestions: What does the owner mean by 'kite workshop'? This file assumes kitesurfing lessons (Kiteboarding Croatia at Ždrijac). If they mean a kite-making or kite-flying workshop for kids, no such offer was found.
Is 'Pag – life on Mars' the Metajna 'Life on Mars' trail (assumed here), the March trail race, or a specific tour the owner has done? A recommended guide or operator would help.
Does Surfmania (or any windsurf station) still operate at Kraljičina plaža next to Sabunike? surfmania.hr no longer resolves.
Is there any SUP or kayak rental in Nin or Privlaka? If not, would the villa keep boards for guests? That would be a strong family and couples selling point.
Which cove is the 'Duboka Draga' snorkeling spot: the OSM beach at Vrsi (44.26882, 15.24613), the bay at 44.29517, 15.17558, or a beach on Vir?
Is supervised mud therapy (peloid) still offered in Nin in July and August, and by whom?
Who runs the Zaton dolphin trip and the Nin horse riding / donkey farm? Does the owner have local contacts or partner discounts to offer guests?
Is the owner willing to arrange transfers (e.g. to Zrće, Zadar boat departures, Paklenica)? Copy currently avoids promising any.
Can the owner confirm the meaning of 'sabunjari' and its link to the name Sabunike before it is used in marketing copy?
Does Kraljevski Vinogradi operate seasonally (its site showed 'Closed – 1.11.2025')? Would it host a private tasting for a villa buy-out group?
Exact driving times from the villa to Ždrijac, Zaton, Pag/Metajna, Zrće, Paklenica, Kaštel Žegarski and Zadar quay should be measured (e.g. OSRM) before publishing.
